subject: Career
title: Freelancer Rate Setting
description: A quick, practical guide to Freelancer Rate Setting.

hook.text: A freelancer charges $50/hour. Their full-time equivalent would earn $120K. They're massively underpaid.

buildup.text: Freelancers must cover taxes, insurance, retirement, equipment, and unbilled hours.

discovery.text: The rule of thumb: your hourly rate should be roughly 2-3x what a salaried employee earns per hour.

twist.text: Clients compare your rate to employee costs. Educating them on total cost prevents sticker shock.

climax.text: Project-based pricing often beats hourly — it ties pay to value, not time.

punchline.text: Freelancers: charge for the value, not the hours.

quiz.question: How should freelance rates compare to equivalent salaried hourly pay?
options: 2-3x higher to cover taxes and benefits

details.summary: Freelancer rate setting requires calculating a target annual income, adding overhead costs for taxes, benefits, and unbillable hours, and then translating that total into hourly, daily, or project-based prices. Most freelancers underprice by failing to account for the full cost of self-employment.
details.whyItMatters: Underpricing erodes freelancer sustainability and devalues the market for peers. Accurate rate setting ensures profitability while communicating professional confidence.
takeaways: Add thirty to fifty percent to target salary for freelance overhead
Account for unbillable hours including admin, learning, and sales
Raise rates annually and communicate increases to existing clients

faq.question: How do I calculate an appropriate freelance hourly rate?
faq.answer: Start with your target annual income, add thirty to fifty percent for taxes, health insurance, retirement, and equipment. Divide by estimated billable hours, typically around 1,200 to 1,500 per year after accounting for vacation and admin time.

faq.question: Should I charge hourly or switch to project-based pricing?
faq.answer: Project-based pricing often earns more because it rewards efficiency rather than time spent. Start with hourly to learn how long tasks take, then transition to project pricing once you can accurately estimate scope and deliver consistently.
